facts.statement: Neovenator fossils are primarily found in the Early Cretaceous Wessex Formation on the south coast of the Isle of Wight, southern England.
facts.quote: It is known primarily from several skeletons found in the Early Cretaceous (Hauterivian–Barremian) Wessex Formation on the south coast of the Isle of Wight, southern England.

facts.statement: The first remains of Neovenator were discovered in 1978 after a collapse at Grange Chine.
facts.quote: The first remains of Neovenator were discovered in 1978 alongside those of the ornithopod Brighstoneus, after the collapse of part of Grange Chine.

facts.statement: The genus Neovenator was named in 1996 by Steve Hutt, David Martill, and Michael Barker.
facts.quote: In 1996, Steve Hutt, David Martill and Michael Barker named the genus Neovenator.

facts.statement: The only known species is N. salerii, named after the Salero family who owned the discovery site.
facts.quote: One species is known: the type species, N. salerii, after the Salero family who owned the site on which its remains were discovered.

facts.statement: Neovenator was likely around 7 meters long and weighed 1 metric ton, though one possibly referable specimen suggests a size of 10 meters.
facts.quote: While incompletely known, it was likely around 7 m in length and probably weighed 1 MT, though a specimen possibly referable to the genus indicates a larger body size of 10 m.

facts.statement: Bite marks on a Mantellisaurus fossil suggest Neovenator preyed on this iguanodontid dinosaur.
facts.quote: Bite marks found on a fossil of the iguanodontid Mantellisaurus suggest that it was among Neovenators prey base.

facts.statement: Neovenator lived during the Barremian stage of the Early Cretaceous, approximately 125 million years ago.
facts.quote: The rocks consisted of plant debris bed L9 within the variegated clays and marls of the Wessex Formation, dating from the Barremian stage of the Early Cretaceous, about 125 million years ago.

facts.statement: The first bones of Neovenator were discovered in the summer of 1978 following a storm-induced collapse at Grange Chine.
facts.quote: The first bones of Neovenator were discovered in the summer of 1978 when a storm made part of the Grange Chine collapse.

facts.statement: The type species Neovenator salerii was named and described in 1996 by Steve Hutt, David Martill, and Michael Barker.
facts.quote: In 1996, Steve Hutt, David Martill and Michael Barker named and described the type species Neovenator salerii.

facts.statement: Teeth possibly belonging to Neovenator were found in 2012 in the Angeac-Charente bone bed in France, dating to the Berriasian.
facts.quote: In 2012, teeth indistinguishable from those associated with the holotype of Neovenator were found in the Angeac-Charente bone bed, in France, dating to the Berriasian.

facts.statement: A position within the clade Carcharodontosauria was first suggested in 1998 and supported by comparative morphology and phylogenetic analyses.
facts.quote: A position within the related clade Carcharodontosauria was first suggested in 1998, and subsequently saw support using both comparative morphology and phylogenetic analyses.

facts.statement: In 2010, Neovenator was assigned to its own family, Neovenatoridae.
facts.quote: In 2010, it was assigned to a family of its own, Neovenatoridae.

facts.statement: The taxonomic position of Neovenator remains a subject of debate.
facts.quote: The taxonomic position of Neovenator has been a subject of debate.

facts.statement: Neovenator was a mid-sized, lightly built carcharodontosaurid.
facts.quote: Neovenator was a mid-sized, lightly built carcharodontosaurid.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen measured approximately 7 to 7.5 meters in length.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen measured approximately 7–7.5 m in length, and was fairly lightly built.

facts.statement: A hip height of about 2 meters has been suggested for Neovenator.
facts.quote: A hip height of about 2 m has been suggested.

facts.statement: Specimen MIWG 4199 suggests a possible length of about 10 meters, but its position within Neovenator is considered dubious.
facts.quote: Specimen MIWG 4199 indicates an individual with a possible length of about 10 m, though it consists only of a pedal phalanx and its position in Neovenator is dubious.

facts.statement: Teeth associated with the type specimen possess characteristic enamel wrinkles but differ in their precise pattern from other carcharodontosaur teeth.
facts.quote: Teeth found in association with the type specimen of Neovenator, while they do possess the characteristic enamel wrinkles of carcharodontosaur teeth, differ in their precise pattern.

facts.statement: The skull of Neovenator measures 70 cm in length.
facts.quote: The length of the skull is 70 cm.

facts.statement: The premaxillae of Neovenator possess a unique 'pen-in-socket connection' not found in other theropods.
facts.quote: The premaxillae have an additional connection (referred to in 2001 as a "pen-in-socket connection"), by not seen in other theropods.

facts.statement: The preserved left maxilla of Neovenator is approximately 30 cm long and 7.5 cm deep.
facts.quote: The left maxilla, as preserved, measures around 30 cm in length, and 7.5 cm in depth.

facts.statement: The dentary of Neovenator was smooth and lacked rugosities, unlike the maxilla and nasal bones.
facts.quote: Unlike the maxilla and nasal, the dentary of Neovenator was fairly smooth, lacking rugosities, unlike what is seen in taxa like Carcharodontosaurus.

facts.statement: The third alveolus of the Neovenator dentary was enlarged, a trait unique among allosauroids except for Acrocanthosaurus.
facts.quote: The third alveolus of the dentary was enlarged, which is unique among allosauroids, save for Acrocanthosaurus.

facts.statement: The preserved premaxilla of Neovenator has five tooth sockets, while the maxilla has fifteen, though more may have been present.
facts.quote: As preserved, Neovenators premaxilla has five alveoli (tooth sockets), as in Allosaurus; its maxilla bears fifteen, though at least one or two more are likely to have been present.

facts.statement: No erupted teeth are known from the Neovenator holotype, but four replacement teeth are preserved.
facts.quote: No teeth are preserved in the premaxilla or maxilla, and no erupted teeth are known from the dentary, though four replacement teeth are preserved.

facts.statement: Neovenator teeth were typical for theropods but differed from other carcharodontosaurs in enamel wrinkle details.
facts.quote: Neovenators teeth were fairly typical for theropod teeth, though differ from those of other carcharodontosaurs in details of the enamel wrinkles.

facts.statement: The holotype of Neovenator preserves six cervical vertebrae and twelve dorsal vertebrae.
facts.quote: Six cervical (neck) vertebrae, including the axis (the second cervical vertebra positionally), are known, as are twelve dorsal (back) vertebrae.

facts.statement: Twenty-three caudal vertebrae are known from the Neovenator holotype.
facts.quote: Also known are twenty-three caudal (tail) vertebrae.

facts.statement: Neovenator is the only known allosauroid in which the rearward cervical vertebrae are fused with their cervical ribs.
facts.quote: The more rearward cervical vertebrae were fused with their cervical ribs; while this is known in many other theropod clades, Neovenator is the only allosauroid in which this was the case.

facts.statement: The second and third sacral vertebrae of Neovenator were fused, a trait shared with some Allosaurus specimens but not Acrocanthosaurus or Sinraptor.
facts.quote: The second and third sacral vertebrae were fused, unlike Acrocanthosaurus and Sinraptor, but like some specimens of Allosaurus.

facts.statement: The holotype of Neovenator preserves nearly complete left scapula and coracoid bones, but the forelimbs are not known.
facts.quote: The left scapula and coracoid of Neovenators holotype are nearly complete, though its forelimbs are not known.

facts.statement: The scapula of Neovenator occupies around two-thirds of the length of the glenoid fossa.
facts.quote: Around two-thirds of the glenoid fossa's length is taken up by the scapula.

facts.statement: The ilium of Neovenator is highly pneumatized.
facts.quote: The ilium overall is highly pneumatised.

facts.statement: The pubis of Neovenator expands distally into a large pubic boot similar to those of other carcharodontosaurs and tyrannosaurids.
facts.quote: Distally, it expands into a large pubic boot, similar to that of other carcharodontosaurs and tyrannosaurids.

facts.statement: The ischiac feet of Neovenator are connected anteriorly, diverge posteriorly, and are expanded, a trait seen in other carcharodontosaurs.
facts.quote: The "feet" of the ischia are connected anteriorly but diverge posteriorly; the ischiac feet were expanded, another trait observed in other carcharodontosaurs.

facts.statement: The femoral head of Neovenator is angled dorsomedially, a trait shared with other carcharodontosaurs and some tyrannosaurids.
facts.quote: Like in other carcharodontosaurs, and in some tyrannosaurids, Neovenators femoral head is angled dorsomedially (upwards and towards the centrum).

facts.statement: The fourth trochanter of Neovenator features a thumbprint-shaped depression on its lateral dorsal border.
facts.quote: The fourth trochanter has a depression in the form of a thumbprint located laterally on its dorsal border.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that the snout of Neovenator was highly vascularized or innervated.
facts.quote: It has been suggested that Neovenators snout was highly vascularised or innervated.

facts.statement: Researchers suggested in 1996 that Neovenator was closely related to Allosaurus and possibly a member of the family Allosauridae.
facts.quote: In the 1996 paper describing Neovenator, Hutt, Martill and Barker suggested a close relationship with Allosaurus, and that Neovenator might itself have been a member of Allosauridae.

facts.statement: A 2000 phylogenetic analysis by Thomas R. Holtz Jr. recovered Neovenator as the sister taxon to Allosaurus.
facts.quote: The first analysis to include Neovenator was published in 2000 by Thomas R. Holtz Jr., and indeed recovered as the sister taxon to Allosaurus.

facts.statement: Benson, Carrano, and Brusatte erected the family Neovenatoridae to include Neovenator and megaraptorans.
facts.quote: Therefore, Benson, Carrano and Brusatte erected the family Neovenatoridae, to encompass both taxa.

facts.statement: Fernando Novas et al. (2013) placed Neovenator at the base of Carcharodontosauridae in a polytomy with Eocarcharia and Concavenator.
facts.quote: Fernano Novas et al. (2013) recovered Neovenator at the base of Carcharodontosauridae, in a polytomy with Eocarcharia and Concavenator.

facts.statement: Researchers suggested Neovenator possessed integumentary sensory organs on its snout based on neurovascular structures found in the skull.
facts.quote: Chris Barker and colleagues suggested that Neovenator may have possessed integumentary sensory organs on its snout, much as modern waterfowl and crocodilians use to find food in muddy water, based on neurovascular structures found on the skull.

facts.statement: Because Neovenator was terrestrial, researchers assume its sensory organs were used for sensing pressure, temperature, and controlling jaw pressure rather than finding food in water.
facts.quote: As Neovenator is believed to be completely terrestrial, unlike the modern species, it is assumed that these sensory organs were used for other purposes, such as sensitivity to pressure and temperature, controlling jaw pressure and precision feeding.

facts.statement: Researchers hypothesize Neovenator may have used sensory organs for courtship and sensing nest conditions.
facts.quote: Additionally, Neovenator might have used these integumentary sensory organs in courtship and sensing nest conditions, a technique seen today in most species of crocodilians and megapode birds.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Neovenator salerii exhibited significant pathology similar to that seen in Allosaurus.
facts.quote: As with many specimens of Allosaurus, the holotype of Neovenator salerii was highly pathological.

facts.statement: Pathologies in the Neovenator holotype included fused caudal vertebrae, healed gastralia fractures, a scapula fracture, regrown gastralium, and osteophytes on foot bones.
facts.quote: The pathologies listed in the 1996 paper and the 2008 monograph: are the fusion of two caudal vertebrae and their associated chevron into a single mass (also seen in certain Allosaurus and likely the result of neoplastic ankylosis); healed fractures to the gastralia; a fracture to the scapula; one gastralium which appears to exhibit regrowth across its entire length, and osteophytes on some of the pedal (foot) phalanges.

facts.statement: Definite Neovenator remains are from the Barremian-age Wessex Formation of the Isle of Wight, while teeth from the Berriasian-age Angeac-Charente bone bed in France may also belong to the genus.
facts.quote: The only definite remains of Neovenator are known from the Barremian-age Wessex Formation of the Isle of Wight, though teeth identical to the genus are known from the Berriasian-age Angeac-Charente bone bed in France.

facts.statement: The Wessex Formation environment was a floodplain intersected by river and lake deposits.
facts.quote: Sedimentological data suggests that the depositional environment of the Wessex Formation was a floodplain intersected by fluvial (river) and lacustrine (lake) deposits.

facts.statement: Evidence of burned plant material suggests the environment experienced frequent wildfires that limited gymnosperm growth.
facts.quote: Burned plant and insect material and fusain suggests that the environment experienced frequent wildfires, stifling for the most part the dense growth of gymnosperms.

facts.statement: The flora consisted mainly of low-lying pteridophytes with occasional conifers, cycads, and the tree fern Tempskya.
facts.quote: Much of the flora of the formed of low ground cover, consisting primarily of pteridophytes, with occasional stands of conifers, cycads and the tree fern Tempskya.

facts.statement: Bite marks provide evidence that Neovenator preyed on Mantellisaurus.
facts.quote: There is evidence in the form of bite marks that Neovenator likely preyed on Mantellisaurus.

facts.statement: Researchers noted in 2001 that Neovenator likely hunted via ambush due to limb proportions unsuited for high speeds.
facts.quote: Darren Naish, Steve Hutt and David Martill noted in 2001 that allosauroids in general had limb proportions poorly suited for great speeds, and that Neovenator likely would have hunted through ambush.

facts.statement: Researchers speculated that Neovenator may have hunted large prey in groups, similar to crocodilians and Komodo dragons.
facts.quote: They speculated that, like what has been suggested for other allosauroids, Neovenator may have ganged up on large prey in a similar fashion to certain crocodilians and Komodo dragons.

facts.statement: The holotype of Neovenator was found in a plant debris bed sandwiched between sandstone and mudstone layers.
facts.quote: The holotype of Neovenator was recovered from a plant debris bed, underlain by sandstone and mudstone, and overlain by further mudstone.

facts.statement: Neovenator fossils were discovered alongside fossil logs, Unionidae bivalves, and a partial skeleton of the dinosaur Brighstoneus.
facts.quote: Its remains were found in association with multiple fossil logs, bivalves of the family Unionidae, and a partial skeleton of the iguanodontid Brighstoneus.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that Neovenator and Brighstoneus remains were likely mixed together by sedimentary pulses caused by floods.
facts.quote: it is likely that the two specimens were swept together by one of two sedimentary pulses (one indicative of a small flood, the other indicative of a far larger flood) which formed the locality.

facts.quote: Parent group: Neovenatoridae

facts.quote: Family: Neovenatoridae

facts.statement: Neovenator is classified as a reptile.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.quote: Type species: Neovenator salerii

facts.quote: Time range: Barremian to Barremian (125.77 to 121.4 million years ago)
